governance_note: Every flag Plumb raises is something it noticed, not something it did. Confidence under 90 means a human has to look. No exceptions.

flags.summary: The document for the Badge component in the Rails port is missing the 'link' variant, which is present in the official documentation.
flags.evidence: "ghost" is listed as a variant but "link" is not mentioned, even though it's part of the official set.
flags.proposed_action: Add the 'link' variant to the list of available variants for the Badge component.
flags.plain: Include 'link' in the list of badge variants.

flags.summary: The document uses 'default' as a variant name, which differs from the official 'default' variant in the official documentation.
flags.evidence: '- default – primary information and active states'
flags.proposed_action: Align with the official terminology by using 'default' instead of 'default – primary information and active states'.
flags.plain: Use 'default' as the variant name, not 'default – primary information and active states'.

patch.before: - default – primary information and active states

flags.false_positive_note: False alarm, kept on purpose. This flag says the "default" variant doesn't match the official "default" variant. Same name. What tripped the scorer is that the mirror writes a short description after the name ("default – primary information and active states"), and it compared that whole line to the bare official name. It flagged a variant that was never wrong. Real finding, real miss, kept visible because a queue that hides its own mistakes teaches you to stop reading the evidence.

flags.summary: The official documentation for Badge lacks guidance on when and why to use each variant.
flags.evidence: "Available in both Base UI and Radix UI variants." - This statement does not explain the rationale or appropriate usage scenarios for these variants.
flags.proposed_action: Add a section explaining the intended use cases for each variant.
flags.plain: Explain when to use default, secondary, destructive, outline, ghost, and link badges.

patch.after:
- Default: Use for standard informational badges.
- Secondary: For less critical information or actions.
- Destructive: To indicate danger or negative outcomes.
- Outline: For a more subtle appearance.
- Ghost: To blend into the background.
- Link: For interactive elements styled as badges.

flags.summary: An example renders Badge as a clickable control, but Badge is non-interactive.
flags.evidence: The docs show Badge used inside an interactive pattern without stating that Badge is presentational. A reader could ship it as a button and break keyboard and screen-reader access for every consumer who copies the example.
flags.proposed_action: Add a 'When not to use' note: Badge is non-interactive; for a clickable state use Button. Update any example that implies otherwise.
flags.plain: Say plainly that Badge isn't clickable, and point people to Button when they need that.

patch.after:
## When not to use

Badge is non-interactive. For a clickable state, use a `Button`.

flags.illustrative_note: Authored, not from the model. The three flags above came from a local model reading the actual docs; that run produced no high-severity finding, so this one is hand-written to show how Plumb treats a high-blast-radius change. A high-severity flag stays with a human at any autonomy setting and needs a deliberate confirmation to approve. Only this flag's wording is authored; the decision flow around it is the real thing.
